lessons.title: Planning a livestock move
lessons.html:
Why planning matters

Moving cattle, sheep, goats or pigs from one farm, camp or auction to another is one of the most stressful events in an animal's life. Poor planning causes bruising, weight loss, injuries, deaths and lost income. As a supervisor you are responsible for the welfare of the animals from the moment they are gathered until they are offloaded. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes it an offence to convey animals in a way that causes them unnecessary suffering.

Before the day of the move

  • Fitness to travel: only load animals that can stand and walk normally. Do not load animals that are sick, injured, lame, very weak, or heavily pregnant and close to giving birth. Ask your vet when in doubt.
  • Paperwork: carry proof of ownership and the required movement documents, such as a stock removal certificate and any veterinary or health declarations required for the area. Animals must be marked or branded according to the farm's identification system.
  • Disease control: check whether you are moving into or out of a disease control area (for example foot-and-mouth disease areas). Movement restrictions under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 must be followed.
  • Route and timing: plan the shortest safe route, rest stops, and travel during the cooler part of the day in summer.
  • Vehicle choice: pick a truck or trailer that suits the type and number of animals.

Feed and water before loading

Animals should be rested and have had access to water before the trip. Many farmers hold animals off heavy feed for a few hours before loading so that they travel with less dung and urine, but water should not be withheld for long. Follow your farm's procedure and the advice of your vet or the transporter.

Selecting the team

Choose handlers who are calm and experienced. Brief them on the plan: who gathers, who works the loading ramp, who closes the gates and who drives. Make sure each person knows the stop signals and the safety rules. A quiet, well-organised team moves animals faster than a shouting one.

lessons.title: Loading, travelling and offloading
lessons.html:
Preparing the vehicle

Inspect the truck or trailer before animals arrive. Check the floor for holes and slippery spots, make sure there is non-slip matting, sand or sawdust, and check that partitions, gates and latches work. There must be no sharp edges, protruding bolts or broken boards. Ventilation openings must be clear. Clean and, where required, disinfect the vehicle, especially if it carried animals from another farm.

Loading

  • Use a solid loading ramp with side walls and a gentle slope. Line the ramp up with the vehicle so there are no gaps for legs to slip through.
  • Move animals quietly using the flight zone and point of balance. Use flags, boards or rattle paddles. Never use sticks to beat animals, never twist tails and never kick or drag animals.
  • Electric prodders, if allowed at all on your farm, may only be used on the hindquarters of adult cattle that refuse to move and have space to move forward. Never use them on calves, sheep, goats or on the face, udder or genitals.
  • Load the correct number per compartment. Overcrowding leads to animals going down and being trampled; too few animals lets them be thrown around.
  • Separate horned from polled cattle, bulls from cows, and small animals from large ones.

During the trip

The driver must drive smoothly, brake and corner gently, and stop at planned intervals to check the load. If an animal is down, stop in a safe place and try to get it up or move it to a separate compartment. On long trips plan for water and rest according to the transport code your industry follows.

Offloading

Offload as soon as possible after arrival, using a ramp of the right height. Let the animals walk off at their own pace into a pen with water and shade. Check every animal for injuries and record any losses or problems.

lessons.title: Safety, records and handling problems
lessons.html:
People safety

Loading livestock is dangerous for people. Cattle can kick, crush you against a wall, or charge. Under the Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 the employer must provide a safe workplace and workers must follow safe procedures.

  • Always have an escape route when working in pens and on the ramp.
  • Never stand directly behind a horse or cow, and never get into a crowded compartment with large animals.
  • Wear safety boots and keep loose clothing tied.
  • Be extra careful with bulls, rams, boars and cows with calves.

Common problems and what to do

ProblemAction
Animal refuses the rampCheck for shadows, puddles or noise ahead; let a calm lead animal go first
Animal goes down in transitStop safely, give it space to stand, separate it if needed
Heat stress (panting, open mouth)Park in shade, keep moving air, offload and give water as soon as possible
Injured animal on arrivalIsolate, record, call the vet

Records

Keep a record of every movement: date, origin, destination, number and type of animals, identification marks, vehicle registration, driver, departure and arrival times, and any deaths or injuries. These records help with traceability during disease outbreaks, stock theft investigations and insurance claims.

After the move

Clean the vehicle and ramp. Watch newly arrived animals for a few days for signs of illness, and keep them apart from the existing herd if your biosecurity plan requires it.

Key points

  • Only fit, healthy animals may be loaded; the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 forbids causing unnecessary suffering.
  • Carry the correct ownership and movement documents and obey disease control rules.
  • Check the vehicle for a non-slip floor, sound partitions and good ventilation.
  • Load quietly at the correct density and separate animals by size, sex and horn status.
  • Always keep an escape route and never stand in a crowded compartment.
  • Record every move for traceability.

quiz.question: Which animal should NOT be loaded for transport?

options.text: A lame cow that cannot walk normally
A dry ewe in good condition
A fit young bull in a separate compartment

quiz.question: What is the main risk of overcrowding a truck compartment?

options.text: Animals go down and are trampled

quiz.question: Which floor is best for a livestock vehicle?

options.text: A floor with holes for drainage
A sound floor with non-slip matting, sand or sawdust

quiz.question: An animal refuses to walk up the ramp. What should you check first?

options.text: Shadows, puddles or noise ahead that may frighten it
Whether a stick will make it move faster
Whether its tail can be twisted

quiz.question: Why should every livestock movement be recorded?

options.text: For traceability in disease outbreaks, stock theft and insurance claims
To replace the need for branding

quiz.question: Horned and polled cattle should be separated when loading.
It is safe for a handler to climb into a crowded compartment of adult cattle to fix a problem.
Which of these should be checked before animals arrive at the vehicle? (select all that apply)

options.text: No sharp edges or protruding bolts
